passages.label: A
passages.text: Many people meet a cookie choice when they open a website. A box may ask whether the site can store information on a phone or computer. This choice can feel small, especially when a person wants to read an article or watch a video quickly. Yet it is useful to pause and ask what will be stored, why it is needed and how long it may remain. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office gives advice on how services should tell people about their use of cookies and on when users must be asked for permission.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A browser offers several controls. A person can delete all cookies, block all cookies or allow all cookies. They can also block third-party cookies, clear cookies when the browser closes, or use a private-browsing session. These are choices about what a browser will store locally. They do not mean that every online action becomes secret. For example, a private session can avoid storing local data such as cookies and browsing history. But the ICO warns that this feature has limits in a privacy context.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The best setting depends on the task. Someone using a school computer program may want a site to remember a language or other preference. On a smartphone, storing a choice can save steps when the site next asks a user to sign in with an email address. On a shared device, someone reading news may want to clear cookies afterwards. Blocking every cookie can make some services less convenient, while allowing every one gives more organisations a chance to collect data. To improve privacy, users can look at which settings suit this visit and this device.

passages.label: D
passages.text: When a person uses a laptop, a tablet or another mobile device to go online, the browser may store a small file about the visit. A downloaded app can have separate controls. A site can remember when you log in. It can also try to collect information for an advert. You may be able to turn off some of that activity in the browser. Keep your password private, especially if you share a computer. Check your choices again when you use a different device.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Good online security is wider than any single button. Browser settings can help a person manage stored cookies, but they should also use care when choosing what to download, signing in, or entering personal details, whether using a keyboard or a touch screen. A browser can record some local information, and users can review its controls from time to time. The aim is not to fear every cookie. It is to make a choice with enough information to understand both the useful result and the possible trade-off.

R_H2.passageTitle: A Second Step for Your Account

passages.label: A
passages.text: A password is often the first lock on an online account, but it is not the only possible lock. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, says that strong passwords alone are no longer enough when used by themselves. A person may use the same password in more than one place, or an attacker may try to obtain it through a false message. For this reason, many services offer multifactor authentication, usually called MFA. It asks for two or more ways to show that the person signing in is really the account holder.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The first proof might be something a person knows, such as a password typed on a keyboard or a touch screen. The second proof might come from an app on a smartphone or from a security key. A website sometimes sends a code to a person's email address as a different check. All these methods are meant to make it harder for a person with just one of the checks to enter.

passages.label: C
passages.text: This extra step can improve account security because an attacker who has one factor may still fail the second check. CISA explains that MFA is useful for email, financial services, social media, online stores and gaming or streaming services. These examples matter because one person may use several accounts in a day. Instead of treating all accounts as equally important, users can begin with accounts that hold valuable details or can be used to reset other passwords. Before you log in on a borrowed laptop or tablet, check whether it expects a code on a mobile device. Store any recovery information where only you can read the file.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Checks differ in how they work. An authenticator app is a computer program that may give a new number at regular intervals. Some versions are free to download. A service can record when someone tries to sign in so a notice may arrive if the activity appears unusual. An advert that asks you to install an app is a different thing from a sign-in request you started. Check the service's own explanation before adding an app. A password should remain secret, and accounts with important information are good places to improve security first.

passages.label: E
passages.text: MFA does not remove every risk or replace careful thinking. People still need to notice unexpected sign-in requests and protect the devices they use. A service may collect account details for a real purpose, but users should check which service is asking and why. Security choices can affect daily habits: signing in may take a few more seconds, yet it can add protection to important accounts. The useful lesson is to understand the extra check and use it where it is available.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A colourful advert can draw a family's interest, especially when it offers a free game for a smartphone, and a family has a useful question to ask before they download it. Which facts come from the promotion and which can be checked elsewhere? The Entertainment Software Rating Board, known as the ESRB, offers information about what is in a game and what a player may meet while playing online. For a family comparing two games, that information is a starting point.

passages.label: B
passages.text: An ESRB rating has three parts. Categories including Everyone and Teen give a guide to age appropriateness. Content descriptors tell people about things including violence or strong language. Interactive elements give other information. They describe functions like purchases within the game, contact with other users, location sharing and open access to the internet. These elements do not set the age category. Two games with the same category can give a family different choices about contact with others.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The ESRB lets families look up a rating on its website or in an app, and a short advert may say the game is educational or show a creative world. A label tells whether certain content or functions are present. Neither one by itself tells a family whether the game gives the player enough room to use their imagination. That is easier to discuss after watching a part of the game or trying it together. Families can do the same research on a laptop or in the rating app before they go online to buy a game. Consider who will use the tablet and which password controls permission to purchase.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A family can also look at what the computer program asks a player to do. On a touch screen, the action may feel different from using a keyboard. Some games ask for an email address or permission to collect information such as location, and those choices affect security and privacy. The family can see which information the game can record, and decide what they would prefer to keep secret.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A game that looks suitable can still leave choices about money, time and communication, and some families use controls on the device to decide which purchases or contacts are possible. The age label, a look at actual play and the information about what the game collects answer different questions. Putting those facts together can improve a family's decision about which game to try and what to check when they start. A parent can make a short list before getting a game, and one item might be whether a player can talk to other people. The family can check that item separately for each game they are thinking about.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can the rating information add when an advertisement has already made a game look attractive?
options: A guarantee that every player will enjoy the same part of the game.
A way to confirm the game will always be as easy as it looks.
Information about what is in the game and what a player can encounter online.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Two games have the same age category, but one gives a family a different decision to make. Which case illustrates this?
options: One game has a different age category, which explains the difference by itself.
Only one permits contact with other users, so the family may treat communication differently.
Both games offer the same kinds of contact, so the age category must go up.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which part of the rating would help someone check whether the player can talk to other users?
options: The descriptor for the language used in dialogue.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which example gives two details that belong to different parts of the rating?
options: Violence and the strength of its language, both as examples of purchases.
A description of violent material and a separate entry about buying items inside the game.
The age category and content label, both described as methods of talking to other users.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A family has checked a sales pitch and looked up formal information. What still needs a different kind of evidence?
options: Whether a displayed statement belongs to a category describing age.
Whether a rating can be recorded separately from the price.
How much room a player gets to invent things while actually using the game.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Where can a family look up the rating apart from reading the advert?
options: Only on the purchase confirmation after the game has been played.
On the ESRB website or in its app.
By asking the other players to decide what the age category stands for.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What two things might a family compare when a title asks for permission to collect data?
options: The information the game can gather and the information the family prefers to keep private.
The size of the screen and the letter that stands for the age category.
The advertised price and the number of buttons on an unrelated keyboard.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can relatives do to put a limit on spending into effect?
options: Leave the decision to the age category without changing anything else.
Ask the game to make every decision based on the current price.
Use device controls to decide which purchases are allowed.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why does the text advise checking actual play as well as the age recommendation and data collection?
options: The sources answer different questions, and comparing them can improve the choice.
Information about which data is collected already answers every question about play.
A different way of playing means the age category no longer has any meaning.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which approach would make the most complete use of the information when choosing a game?
options: Trust the short introduction until the time comes to make a purchase, then read only the age category.
Use the rating to learn what is offered, see how play works, and decide what payments, communication or sharing to allow.
Watch someone play and assume that how it looks is all that matters for every member of the household.
